questions.html: Which cache mapping function does not require a replacement algorithm?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 3)

When a new block of data comes from memory, but the cache is already full, the cache must decide which old block to throw out. This decision rule is called a replacement algorithm.

  • In a direct-mapped cache, each memory block can go to exactly one location in the cache (it’s “mapped directly”).

  • So when a new block comes in, it must overwrite the old block at that exact spot.

  • No choice = no replacement policy required.

questions.html: Which cache mapping function is least likely to thrash, i.e., it has the lowest chance of two blocks contending with each other to be stored in the same line?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 4)

Thrashing means two (or more) memory blocks keep replacing each other again and again because they are forced to go to the same cache line.

Fully associative cache has the lowest chance of thrashing because any block can go into any cache line. There’s no fixed slot, so blocks rarely evict each other unless the entire cache is full.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

In direct mapped: every contending block fights for 1 line → 100% replacement chance after fill-up.

In 2-way set associative: 3rd block (same set) contends across 2 lines → 50% chance of two blocks contending in the same line (one gets replaced).

In n-way: contention across n lines → 1/n chance (only one replacement out of n eligible).

In fully associative: no set restriction, contention across all cache lines → 1/total_lines chance (one replacement out of maximum eligible lines).

Hence, fully associative has the lowest chance—one replacement out of maximum eligible lines

questions.html: Which is the fastest cache mapping function? ("Fastest" in terms of access/lookup speed)
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

Direct Mapping is the fastest because the mapping is fixed (simple modulo arithmetic). Only one comparator is required to check the tag. Hardware is simple and fast.

Set Associative and Fully Associative require multiple comparisons $\rightarrow$ slower.

questions.html: Which one of the following statements about cache memories is true?

options.html: Fully associative caches offer better latency, while direct-mapped caches have lower miss rates.
Fully associative caches offer lower miss rates, while direct-mapped caches have better latency.
Direct-mapped caches have both better miss rates and better latency.
Both generally have similar latency and miss rates.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 3)

  • Direct-mapped cache → no replacement policy needed.

  • Fully associative cache → least chance of thrashing.

  • Direct-mapped cache → fastest lookup (lowest latency).

  • Fully associative cache → lower miss rate; Direct-mapped cache → better latency.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Latency:  the time from when the CPU requests a piece of data to when that data is actually delivered is called latency. 
In direct- mapped cache, we need to check only one cache line for a given address. Whereas for fully associative cache requires searching all caches simultaneously. 

Miss rates: Fully associative caches have the lowest miss rates because a block can be placed anywhere in the cache, reducing conflict misses. Direct-mapped caches have higher miss rates because each block has only one possible location, leading to more conflict misses.

questions.html: Consider a $256$ KB $4$-way set associative cache with $256$ byte cache lines for a processor that uses $64$-bit data words and $48$-bit byte addresses. What is the size (in bits) of the tag field per cache block?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

64 -bit word $/ 8$ bits per byte $=8$ bytes per word $\Rightarrow 3$ bits to select byte in word 256 byte line $/ 8$ bytes per word $=32$ words per line $\Rightarrow 5$ bits to select word in line 256 k cache $/ 256$ bytes per line $/ 4$ ways per set $=256$ sets $\Rightarrow 8$ bits to select set The rest of the bits are the tag $\Rightarrow 32$ bit tag.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
47:16 & 15:8 & 7:3 & 2:0 \\
\hline
\text{tag} & \text{set} & \text{word in line} & \text{byte in word} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Given , 48bit byte addresses. Means total  address space is 48bits.

 • 256 bytes cache lines which means each cache line (block) is of 256 bytes i.e, block offset equals to 256bytes = 8 bits.

       • 256kB is the cache size therefore no of cache lines is equal to (cache size/cache block size) = 256kb/256 = 2^10 lines

        •In cache there are 2^10 lines for index bits 2^10/4(since 4 way set associative) = 2^8.

8 bits for offset.

8bits for index.

Finally tag bits = 48bits-8bits(index)-8bits(offset)

32 bits remaining for tag bits.

Therefore 32 is the answer.

Source solution 3 (score: 2)

Based on the problem provided in the image, here is the step-by-step solution to find the size of the tag field.

 

Given Data:

 

  • Total Cache Size: $256 \text{ KB}$

  • Block Size (Line Size): $256 \text{ bytes}$

  • Associativity: $4$-way set associative

  • Physical Address Size: $48 \text{ bits}$

  • Note: The "$64$-bit data words" is extra information regarding the data bus width and does not affect the address bit calculation because the problem specifies the system uses byte addresses.

 

Step 1: Calculate Block Offset Bits

 

The block offset bits determine the specific byte within a cache block.

 

$$\text{Block Offset} = \log_2(\text{Block Size})$$

$$\text{Block Offset} = \log_2(256) = \log_2(2^8) = \mathbf{8 \text{ bits}}$$

 

Step 2: Calculate the Number of Sets

 

To find the number of index bits, we first need to know how many sets are in the cache.

 

$$\text{Number of Sets} = \frac{\text{Total Cache Size}}{\text{Block Size} \times \text{Associativity}}$$

  • Convert Cache Size to bytes: $256 \text{ KB} = 256 \times 1024 \text{ bytes} = 2^{18} \text{ bytes}$

  • Block Size: $256 \text{ bytes} = 2^8 \text{ bytes}$

  • Associativity: $4 = 2^2$

$$\text{Number of Sets} = \frac{2^{18}}{2^8 \times 2^2} = \frac{2^{18}}{2^{10}} = 2^8 = \mathbf{256 \text{ Sets}}$$

 

Step 3: Calculate Set Index Bits

 

The index bits identify which set the address belongs to.

 

$$\text{Set Index Bits} = \log_2(\text{Number of Sets})$$

$$\text{Set Index Bits} = \log_2(256) = \log_2(2^8) = \mathbf{8 \text{ bits}}$$

 

Step 4: Calculate Tag Bits

 

The physical address is split into Tag, Set Index, and Block Offset.

 

$$\text{Tag Bits} = \text{Total Address Bits} - (\text{Set Index Bits} + \text{Block Offset Bits})$$

$$\text{Tag Bits} = 48 - (8 + 8)$$

$$\text{Tag Bits} = 48 - 16$$

$$\text{Tag Bits} = \mathbf{32 \text{ bits}}$$

 

Final Answer:

 

The size of the tag field per cache block is 32 bits.

questions.html:
Consider a $256$ KB $4$-way set associative cache with $256$ byte cache lines for a processor that uses $64$-bit data words and $48$-bit byte addresses. Assume the variable x, of type uint64_t, is stored in memory at location 0x4A85 B413 A518. (uint64_t means an unsigned $64$-bit integer)
Assume that x is present in the cache, and char* ptr $=0 \times 4 \mathrm{~A} 85$ B400 0000. (Note: sizeof(char) = 1)

Consider the accesses in the following options. For each access, it can be a MISS or HIT or NOT ENOUGH INFO. For each access, it is a MISS if it "must" cause a miss, HIT if it will "never" cause a miss, or NOT ENOUGH INFO.
Determine which of the following accesses will cause a cache HIT.
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
*\left(\mathrm{ptr}+0 \times 11_A538\right) & \text{MISS} & \text{HIT} & \text{(NOT ENOUGH INFO)} \\
*\left(\mathrm{ptr}+0 \times 13_A588\right) & \text{MISS} & \text{(HIT)} & \text{NOT ENOUGH INFO} \\
*\left(\mathrm{ptr}+0 \times 13_0218\right) & \text{MISS} & \text{HIT} & \text{(NOT ENOUGH INFO)} \\
\end{array}
$$

* (ptr + 0x11_A538) is in the same set but has a different tag, it may or may not be in another way in that set. *(ptr + 0x13_A588) is in same the line as $x$ (it is in the same set and has the same tag), and since $x$ in present in the cache, it must be also. *(ptr + 0x13_0218) has the same tag, but is in a different set, so it may or may not be in the cache.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Based on the problem statement and the cache configuration provided in the image, here is the step-by-step solution to determine which access will result in a guaranteed cache HIT.

 

1. Analyze the Cache Configuration

 

First, we need to break down how the 48-bit physical address is interpreted by the cache.

  • Block Offset:

    • Block Size = $256$ bytes = $2^8$ bytes.

    • Offset Bits = 8 bits (Corresponds to the last 2 Hex digits).

  • Set Index:

    • Number of Sets = $\frac{\text{Cache Size}}{\text{Associativity} \times \text{Block Size}}$

    • Number of Sets = $\frac{256 \text{ KB}}{4 \times 256 \text{ Bytes}} = \frac{256 \times 1024}{1024} = 256 \text{ Sets}$.

    • Index Bits = $\log_2(256) = \mathbf{8 \text{ bits}}$ (Corresponds to the 2 Hex digits preceding the offset).

  • Tag:

    • Remaining bits = $48 - (8 \text{ Index} + 8 \text{ Offset}) = 32$ bits.

    • Tag Bits = 32 bits (Corresponds to the first 8 Hex digits).

Address Structure (Hexadecimal):

[ Tag (8 digits) ] [ Index (2 digits) ] [ Offset (2 digits) ]

 

2. Analyze the Address of Variable x

 

We are told that variable x is present in the cache. This means the specific cache block containing x is loaded. For another access to be a guaranteed HIT, it must target the exact same block (i.e., it must have the exact same Tag and Index).

  • Address of x: 0x4A85 B413 A518

  • Breakdown:

    • Offset: 18 (Last 2 digits)

    • Index: A5 (Next 2 digits)

    • Tag: 4A85 B413 (First 8 digits)

Condition for HIT: The target address must have Tag = 4A85 B413 and Index = A5.

 

3. Evaluate the Options

 

We need to calculate the address for each option by adding the offset to the base pointer ptr.

Base ptr address: 0x4A85 B400 0000

Option A: *(ptr + 0x11A538)

  • Calculation: 0x4A85 B400 0000 + 0x11A538 = 0x4A85 B411 A538

  • Breakdown:

    • Offset: 38

    • Index: A5 (Matches x)

    • Tag: 4A85 B411 (Mismatch with x's tag 4A85 B413)

  • Result: Different block. No guaranteed HIT.

Option B: *(ptr + 0x13A588)

  • Calculation: 0x4A85 B400 0000 + 0x13A588 = 0x4A85 B413 A588

  • Breakdown:

    • Offset: 88

    • Index: A5 (Matches x)

    • Tag: 4A85 B413 (Matches x)

  • Result: This address maps to the exact same cache block as x. Since x is present, this block is present. Guaranteed HIT.

Option C: *(ptr + 0x130218)

  • Calculation: 0x4A85 B400 0000 + 0x130218 = 0x4A85 B413 0218

  • Breakdown:

    • Offset: 18

    • Index: 02 (Mismatch with x's index A5)

    • Tag: 4A85 B413

  • Result: Different set. No guaranteed HIT.

 

Conclusion

 

Only the address in Option B has the same Tag and Set Index as variable x. Therefore, it accesses the same cache block that is already known to be in the cache.

Correct Answer: B

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

 

Address Space: 48 bits

Block Size (Line Size): 256 bytes = $2^8$ bytes $\implies$ 8 bits for Block Offset

Cache Size: 256 KB = $2^{18}$ bytes

Total Blocks in Cache: $\frac{256\text{ KB}}{256\text{ B}} = 1024$ blocks

Associativity: 4-way set associative $\implies$ Each set contains 4 blocks.

Total Sets in Cache: $\frac{1024\text{ blocks}}{4} = 256 = 2^8$ sets $\implies$ 8 bits for Set Index

Now we find the Tag bits:

$$\text{Tag bits} = 48 - (\text{Set Index bits} + \text{Block Offset bits}) = 48 - (8 + 8) = 32\text{ bits}$$

$$\text{Address Format: } \underbrace{\texttt{T T T T T T T T}}_{32\text{ bits (Tag)}} \ \underbrace{\texttt{S S}}_{8\text{ bits (Set)}} \ \underbrace{\texttt{O O}}_{8\text{ bits (Offset)}}$$

in hexadecimal format

We know the variable x is currently present in the cache at address 0x4A85 B413 A518. Let's parse it:

  • Tag: 4A85B413

  • Set Index: A5

  • Block Offset: 18

Because x is guaranteed to be in the cache, anyy future access that maps to this exact same Tag and Set Index will cause a Cache HIT.

Given the base pointer: ptr = 0x4A85 B400 0000

Option A

$$\text{Address} = \texttt{0x4A85 B400 0000} + \texttt{0x11 A538} = \texttt{0x4A85 B411 A538}$$

  • Tag: 4A85B411 (Mismatch)

  • Set Index: A5

  • Result: MISS

Option B

$$\text{Address} = \texttt{0x4A85 B400 0000} + \texttt{0x13 A588} = \texttt{0x4A85 B413 A588}$$

  • Tag: 4A85B413 ($\color{green}{\text{Matches!}}$)

  • Set Index: A5 ($\color{green}{\text{Matches!}}$)

  • Result: HIT (Since it targets the exact same memory block currently holding x).

Option C

$$\text{Address} = \texttt{0x4A85 B400 0000} + \texttt{0x13 0218} = \texttt{0x4A85 B413 0218}$$

  • Tag: 4A85B413

  • Set Index: 02 (Mismatch)

  • Result: MISS

questions.html:
Suppose a computer has an $8$-bit address space. It has a $2$-way set-associative cache with LRU replacement policy. Cache size is $64$ Bytes and block size is $8$ Bytes.
What is the length of the tag field (in bits) ?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 2)

  • Address size = 8 bits.

  • Block size = 8 bytes → block offset bits = log⁡2(8)=3

  • Cache size = 64 bytes → number of lines = 64÷8=8

  • 2-way set-associative → number of sets = 8÷2=4

  • Index bits = log⁡2(4)=2

  • Tag bits = 8−3−2=3

questions.html: A direct-mapped cache has $64$ blocks and a block size of $16$ bytes. To what block number in the cache does byte address $1220_{10}$ map?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 7)

First find the main memory block number to which the byte address 1220 belongs to, which can be found by $1220 / 16$, so, block number 76 (NOTE that block numbers start with 0 ).

Now, block number 76 maps to line number $76 \% 64=12$.

Source solution 2 (score: 4)

Answer: 12

Easiest Explaination:

\[
\text{Number of bits for block offset} = \log_2(16) = 4 \text{ bits}
\]

\[
\text{Number of bits for line number} = \log_2(64) = 6 \text{ bits}
\]

\[
(1220)_{10} = (10011000100)_2
\]

\[
\text{Address format: } \quad 1 \;|\; 001100 \;|\; 0100
\]

\[
\text{Line number} = (001100)_2 = (12)_{10}
\]

 

Source solution 3 (score: 1)

  • Question: Block number for address 1220 (64 blocks, 16B block size).

  • Calc:

    1. Block Address = $1220 / 16 = 76$ (integer division).

    2. Cache Block Number = $76 \pmod{64} = 12$.

  • Answer: C. 12

questions.html: The size of the physical address space of a processor is $2^P$ bytes. The word length is $2^W$ bytes. The capacity of cache memory is $2^N$ bytes. The size of each cache block is $2^M$ words. For a $K$-way set-associative cache memory, the length (in number of bits) of the tag field is
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

$\text{Physical Address Space} =2^P$ Bytes, i.e., $P$ bits to represent the size of total memory.

$\text{Cache Size} = 2^N$ Bytes, i.e., $N$ bits to represent Cache memory.

$\text{Tag size} = 2^X$ Bytes, i.e., $X$ bits to represent Tag.

Cache is $K-$way associative.

$\text{(Size of Tag)} \times \frac{\text{Cache Size}}{K} = \text{Total Memory Size}$

$\implies 2^X \times \frac{2^N}{K} = 2^P $

$\implies 2^{X+N-\log(K)} = 2^P $

$\implies 2^{X} = 2^{P-N+\log(K)} $

$\implies X (\text{Size of Tag in bits}) = P - N + \log(K)$

Correct Answer: $B$

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Answer: (B)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\textbf{Physical Address Bits:} \quad
& \log_2(2^P) = P \\[6pt]

\textbf{Block Size:} \quad
& 2^M \text{ words} = 2^M \cdot 2^W = 2^{M+W} \\
& \Rightarrow \text{Block offset bits} = M + W \\[6pt]

\textbf{Number of Lines:} \quad
& \frac{2^N}{2^{M+W}} = 2^{N - M - W} \\[6pt]

\textbf{K-way Set Associative Cache:} \quad
& \text{Number of sets} = \frac{2^{N - M - W}}{K} \\
& \Rightarrow \text{Set index bits} = \log_2\left(\frac{2^{N - M - W}}{K}\right) \\
& = N - M - W - \log_2 K \\[6pt]

\textbf{Let Tag Bits} = x \\[6pt]

\textbf{Address Breakdown:} \quad
& x + \text{Set bits} + \text{Offset bits} = P \\
& x + (N - M - W - \log_2 K) + (M + W) = P \\[6pt]

\textbf{Final Result:} \quad
& x = P - N + \log_2 K
\end{aligned}
\]
